english: Greetings / Touching feet (traditional Pahadi greeting for elders)
usage_notes: Used when greeting elders, grandparents (Baujyu/Aama), or respected persons. The standard loving response from elders is 'Je raya' (जी रया - live long) or 'Bhal hejo' (भल हेजो - may good come to you).

english: Live long and stay happy (Elder's blessing)
usage_notes: Elders respond with this when younger people say 'Pailaag'. Another blessing is 'Daud-dhub panpi jaya' (grow verdant like the grass).
Use 'Kas chhi' for females, 'Kas chha' for males. For elders or polite speech, use 'Kas chho?' (कस छो?).
'Bhal' means good/well. 'Chhu' is the first-person auxiliary verb (I am). For plural or respectful, say 'Ham bhal chhaun' (हम भल छौं).
'Twaar' = your (casual/younger), 'Naun' = name, 'Ke' = what, 'Chha' = is. Polite form: 'Tumhaar naun ke chha?'.
'Myar' = my / mine.

hindi: तुम्हारा घर कहाँ है? / तुम कहाँ के रहने वाले हो?
usage_notes: 'Ghar' = home/village, 'Kaan' = where.

english: My home is in the hills / mountains.
usage_notes: Can substitute with city/village name: 'Myar ghar Almora chha'.
In Kumaon, '-jyu' is a reverent honorific attached to elder kinship terms.
'Ija' is the quintessential Kumaoni word for mother. Often said as 'Eeeja!' in emotional exclamation.

kumaoni: दाज्यू (Dajyu) = बड़ा भाई, भुली (Bhuli) = छोटी बहन, भैल (Bhail) = छोटा भाई, दीदी (Didi) = बड़ी बहन
transliteration: Dajyu (Elder brother), Bhuli (Younger sister), Bhail (Younger brother), Didi (Elder sister)
english: Siblings: Elder brother, Younger sister, Younger brother, Elder sister
usage_notes: 'Dajyu' is famously used across Uttarakhand as a term of brotherly respect.

kumaoni: काका (Kaka) = चाचा, काकी (Kaki) = चाची, मामा (Mama) = मामा, मैमा (Maima) = मामी
transliteration: Kaka (Uncle/Father's brother), Kaki (Aunt), Mama (Maternal Uncle), Maima (Maternal Aunt)
usage_notes: Maternal house is called 'Mamyol' (माम्योल).
In the hills, 'Bhat' (boiled rice) represents the entire midday meal. Asking someone if they've eaten bhat is the primary sign of care.

hindi: काले भट्ट की दाल/सूप और कढ़ी-चावल
english: Black soybean slow-cooked curry (Churkani) and Pahadi buttermilk kadhi (Jholi) with rice
usage_notes: Churkani is cooked in a heavy iron kadhai (lohe ki kadhai) which gives it an iconic dark colour, rich in iron and protein.

hindi: सिलबट्टे पर पिसी दाल के डुबके और कुल्थी (गहत) की दाल
english: Dubke (ground paste dal slow simmered) and Gahat (Horse gram) dal
usage_notes: Gahat is eaten extensively during chilly winters because of its warming properties and medicinal benefits.

hindi: अल्मोड़ा की प्रसिद्ध बाल मिठाई और मालू के पत्ते में लिपटी सिंगौड़ी
english: Almora's roasted brown khoya fudge coated in sugar balls (Baal Mithai) and condensed milk wrapped in Maalu leaves (Singodi)
usage_notes: World-famous desserts originating from Almora, Kumaon.
Mountain hospitality mandates that no guest leaves without a hot cup of sweet, milky ginger tea.

hindi: भांग के बीज और गुड़ के साथ साने हुए पहाड़ी नींबू
english: Pahadi citrus salad prepared with roasted bhang seeds (hemp seed paste), jaggery, curd, and green chilies
usage_notes: Eaten on sunny winter afternoons sitting in the courtyard (Aangan) with family.
Fem: 'Kaan jaanchhi?'. Plural/Polite: 'Kaan jaanchho?'.

hindi: क्या मेले में जा रहे हो?
english: Are you going to the village fair/festival?
usage_notes: 'Koutik' (कौतिक) is the Kumaoni word for a fair/mela (like Nanda Devi Mela or Uttarayani).
'Bhaut' = very / a lot, 'Chha' = is.
'Ghaam' = sunlight / sunshine, 'Taapno' = to warm oneself.
'Hindno' (हिंडण) means to walk. Essential advice on steep hill footpaths (danda).

transliteration: Khaan (To eat) -> Khun chhu (I eat), Khaayo (ate), Khool (will eat)
usage_notes: Main bhat khun chhu (I eat rice).

transliteration: Jaan (To go) -> Jaanchhu (I go), Gyo (went), Jool (will go)
usage_notes: Main school jaanchhu (I go to school). Wo gyo (He went).

transliteration: Aan (To come) -> Aanchhu (I come), Aayo (came), Aul (will come)
usage_notes: Ghar aayo (Came home). Aaya! (Please come - polite).
'Baisa' (बैसा) is a polite invitation to take a seat.
'Kumaoni bola!' = Speak Kumaoni!
'Ya dekha!' = Look here!

kumaoni: सर्वनाम (Pronouns): मैं (Main = I), हम (Ham = We), तू (Tu = You informal), तुम (Tum = You familiar), आप (Aap = You respectful), ऊ (Oo = He/She/That), यो (Yo = This).
transliteration: Main (I), Ham (We), Tu (You), Aap (You formal), Oo (He/She), Yo (This)
usage_notes: Possessive forms: Myar (My), Twaar (Your), Hmaar (Our), Unar (Their), Wokar (His/Her).

kumaoni: सहायक क्रिया 'होना' (Verb To Be): छु (chhu = I am), छा (chha = he is / you are - masc), छी (chhi = she is / you are - fem), छौं (chhaun = we are), छो (chho = you all / formal are).
transliteration: Chhu (am), Chha (is/are - masc), Chhi (is/are - fem), Chhaun (we are), Chho (respectful are)
english: Forms of the auxiliary verb 'To Be' in present tense
usage_notes: Past tense equivalents: Chhiyo (था - was masc), Chhiye (थी - was fem), Chhiya (थे - were).

kumaoni: १ = एक (Ek), २ = दुई (Dui), ३ = तीन (Teen), ४ = चार (Chaar), ५ = पाँच (Paanch), ६ = छ (Chha), ७ = सात (Saat), ८ = आठ (Aath), ९ = नौ (Nau), १० = दस (Das)
transliteration: 1: Ek, 2: Dui, 3: Teen, 4: Chaar, 5: Paanch, 6: Chha, 7: Saat, 8: Aath, 9: Nau, 10: Das
usage_notes: 'Dui' is used for two (e.g., Dui chaa = Two teas).

kumaoni: बुराँश (Buraansh) = लाल रोडोडेंड्रोन (Rhododendron), काफल (Kaafal) = स्वादिष्ट पहाड़ी जंगली बेरी (Bayberry)
hindi: बुरांश का फूल और काफल फल
english: Buraansh (State tree flower used for ruby juice) and Kaafal (Beloved wild sour-sweet summer berry)
usage_notes: Famous hill saying: 'काफल पाको चैत, मेरी छैला' (Kaafal ripens in Chaitra month). Buraansh squash is served to all summer visitors.

kumaoni: बाँज (Baanjh) = बांज / ओक का पेड़ (Himalayan Oak)
usage_notes: Known as the lifeline of Kumaon's ecosystem, retaining natural springs (Naula and Dhaara) and sweet groundwater.

hindi: पारंपरिक जल स्त्रोत (नौला = बावड़ी, धारा = प्राकृतिक झरना)
english: Traditional Himalayan natural aquifer wells (Naula) and natural spring waterspouts (Dhaara)
usage_notes: Naulas are treated with religious sanctity. Shoes are always removed before stepping down to collect sweet hill water.

kumaoni: गाइ (Gai) = गाय, ब्यर (Byar) = बैल, भैस (Bhais) = भैंस, कुकुर (Kukur) = कुत्ता, बिरालो (Biraalo) = बिल्ली, घ्वड़ (Ghwad) = घोड़ा
transliteration: Gai (Cow), Byar (Bullock), Bhais (Buffalo), Kukur (Dog), Biraalo (Cat), Ghwad (Horse)
usage_notes: Kukur = Dog, Biraalo = Cat, Gai = Cow.

kumaoni: बाघ (Bagh) = गुलदार / तेंदुआ (Leopard), भालू (Bhaalu) = हिमालयी काला भालू, घुरड़ (Ghurad) = पहाड़ी हिरण
transliteration: Bagh / Guldar (Leopard), Bhaalu (Himalayan Black Bear), Ghurad (Barking Deer)
english: Wild animals of the Kumaon Himalayas
usage_notes: In the hills, villagers colloquially say 'Bagh aago!' (बाघ आगो!) to warn of leopards near the village cattle shed.

kumaoni: फूलदेई (Phooldei) = छम्मा देई, फूल देई, दैली का द्वार, भर भकार!
transliteration: Phooldei, Chhamma dei, Daili ka dwaar, bhar bhakaar!
hindi: फूलदेई (पहाड़ का बाल पर्व - वसंत ऋतु का स्वागत)
english: Phooldei - Spring harvest flower festival where children place fresh wildflowers on village doorsteps
usage_notes: Celebrated on the first day of the Hindu solar month Chaitra. Children sing blessings wishing granaries (bhakaar) stay full.

kumaoni: हरेला (Harela) = 'जी रया, जागि रया, ती स्यूं जस हरिया रया'
transliteration: Harela: Je raya, jaagi raya, tee syun jas hariya raya
hindi: हरेला पर्व - हरियाली और कृषि उत्सव
english: Harela festival celebrating the monsoon, greenery, and agriculture
usage_notes: Nine types of seeds are germinated in clay pots in the dark. On Harela day, elders place the yellow-green shoots on youth's heads with blessings.

hindi: मकर संक्रांति (घुघुतिया) - 'काले कौवा काले, घुघुति माला खा ले!'
english: Makar Sankranti celebrated by making deep-fried sweet wheat flour twists (ghughuti) for crows and migrating birds
usage_notes: Children string ghughuti twists into edible necklaces and chant to invite crows across the mountain ridges.

kumaoni: ऐपण (Aipan) = गेरू (लाल मिट्टी) और बिस्वार (पिसे चावल के घोल) से बनाई गई पारंपरिक लोक चित्रकला
transliteration: Aipan (Ritual folk art in red geru clay and white rice paste biswaar)
hindi: ऐपण कला (कुमाऊँ की पारंपरिक देहरी और पूजा कला)
english: Aipan - Sacred Kumaoni geometric folk art drawn at doorsteps, chowkis, and temples for prosperity
usage_notes: The characteristic reddish-brown background is made with 'Geru' clay, and motifs like Vasudhaara and feet of Lakshmi are painted with 'Biswaar'.

kumaoni: जै को हुण छ भल, उक नौं घल।
transliteration: Jai ko hun chha bhal, uk naun ghal.
hindi: जिसका भला होना होता है, उसका नाम सब जगह फैल जाता है।
english: One destined for good will find fortune and fame naturally.
usage_notes: A traditional Pahadi Pakhano (proverb) illustrating destiny and honesty.

kumaoni: अंग्वाव में जो छ, उ मुक्काम में नी हुण।
transliteration: Angwaav mein jo chha, u mukkaam mein nee hun.
hindi: जो बात आंगन में है, वह परदेस में कहाँ!
english: The warmth of one's own courtyard cannot be found anywhere in distant foreign lands.
usage_notes: Reflects the deep emotional connection Pahadis feel towards their home village (Mait / Ghar).

hindi: अरे यार / सुना है कि / कहते हैं (बात के अंत में लगने वाला तकियाकलाम)
english: The signature Kumaoni conversational filler tag (like 'you know' / 'they say')
usage_notes: Used at the end of sentences everywhere: 'Kas chha bal?' (What's up, man?), 'Oo aagyo bal!' (He has arrived, apparently!).

hindi: अरे बाप रे! / हे भगवान! (हैरानी या आश्चर्य की अभिव्यक्ति)
english: Exclamation of shock, amusement, or disbelief ('Oh my goodness!')
usage_notes: When something unexpected happens, elders exclaim 'Dhatteri ki!' or call upon their mother 'Eeeja!' in amazement.
